screens.title: Introduction to UMG
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn what Unreal Motion Graphics, or UMG, does and how to use a Widget Blueprint to create a simple HUD that appears during gameplay. UMG is the visual editor inside Unreal Engine for building menus, inventory screens, and heads-up displays without writing C++ code. You'll see how a Widget Blueprint holds UI widgets, how panel widgets like the Canvas Panel control layout, and why anchoring is crucial for responsive positioning across screen sizes. We'll also cover the runtime steps: creating the widget in Blueprint, then adding it to the viewport so the player can see it. A short example you will implement shows a score label and a coin icon anchored to the top-right of the screen. Understanding this flow — design, anchor, create, and add — ensures the UI looks consistent in editor and at runtime. By the end you will be able to make a basic HUD, test it in Play In Editor, and avoid common mistakes such as forgetting to add the widget to the viewport or misusing anchors. Think about one UI you need in your game and how anchoring would keep it stable across window sizes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand UMG's role and be able to create and display a Widget Blueprint. First, you'll know what UMG is and why it is used to build HUDs, menus, and interactive screens without C++ code. Second, you'll create and configure a Widget Blueprint, place common widgets such as Text Block and Image, and arrange them inside panels like the Canvas Panel. Third, you'll apply anchoring and layout principles so your UI remains responsive across resolutions. Finally, you'll connect your UI to gameplay by creating the widget in Blueprint and using Add to Viewport so it renders during play. Each objective maps to a hands-on practice: design a simple HUD, set anchors, and add the widget at Event BeginPlay. These skills matter because players on different devices must see consistent UI, and Blueprints let you iterate quickly. A quick misconception to avoid: creating a widget asset is not enough — you must also add it to the viewport. Keep that in mind as your verification milestone.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Why They Matter
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to tasks you will do during the hands-on activity. You will create a Widget Blueprint asset and add Text and Image widgets to a Canvas Panel. You will practice setting anchors so a 'Score: 0' label and a coin image remain pinned to the top-right corner on varied screen sizes. You will then open your Player Character or Player Controller Blueprint, hook Event BeginPlay to Create Widget with your new Blueprint class, and call Add to Viewport on the returned reference. The why: players experience inconsistent HUDs when anchors are ignored, and widgets that are created but not added remain invisible. A typical beginner mistake is skipping Add to Viewport; another is anchoring the element to the wrong corner so it drifts off-screen on other aspect ratios. Your verified milestone is simple: run Play In Editor and confirm the HUD appears in the expected position on at least two different aspect ratios. If it does, you have successfully completed the core workflow and can iterate further by adding dynamic text updates and icons.

screens.title: What is UMG and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: UMG stands for Unreal Motion Graphics. It is the built-in visual UI system inside Unreal Engine that lets you create menus, HUDs, and interactive screens using Widget Blueprints. Widget Blueprints are assets that contain widgets — the building blocks like text blocks, images, buttons, and progress bars — arranged in panel widgets that control layout. The major practical advantage is iteration speed: designers and scripters can place widgets visually and hook up behavior in Blueprint graphs without compiling engine code. For example, if you need a pause menu or a health display, you can drag a Text Block and an Image into a Widget Blueprint and then update the text from game logic. A common misconception is thinking UMG is only for simple overlays; in fact it supports complex, data-driven UIs, animations, and binding to game variables. However, it’s also important to be mindful of performance: many complex widgets rendered every frame can affect framerate, so use caching or Retainer Boxes when needed. To practice, create a new UserWidget and add a Text Block named HealthText, set default text, and preview in the Designer tab. How would you use UMG to make your game's main menu responsive and extendable?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is UMG and why use it?
Core Concept

UMG: Visual UI design in Unreal

UMG enables you to assemble interactive interfaces in the Designer and connect behavior in Blueprints, avoiding C++ for most UI work.

Definition
UMG is Unreal's system for creating UI using widgets and Widget Blueprints.
Concrete example
Create a UserWidget, add a Text Block named HealthText, set default to "Health: 100" and preview in Designer.
Common misconception
UMG is not only for static overlays; it supports bindings, animations, and Blueprint-driven updates, but be mindful of performance.
Designer preview
Canvas Panel (root)
❤
HealthText
Default: Health: 100

Key Takeaway

UMG lets you build interactive, visually-driven UI quickly with Widget Blueprints; use it to prototype and ship in-game interfaces without engine code.

screens.title: Widget Blueprint explained
screens.narratorSegment: A Widget Blueprint is a special Blueprint asset whose root is typically a panel widget and whose children are UMG widgets such as Text Block, Image, Button, Progress Bar, and more. Think of it as a container that both defines the visual arrangement and exposes a graph where you add logic to react to input or update text and images. In the Designer tab you drag widgets into panels and set properties like name, text, brush textures, size, anchors, and ZOrder. In the Graph tab you can create bindings, events, and functions that change widget properties at runtime. For example, a WBP_PlayerHUD could expose an UpdateHealth function that accepts an integer and sets the HealthText to "Health: " plus that value. A common misconception is that widgets created in the Content Browser automatically appear; they do not. You must create an instance at runtime and call Add to Viewport. When naming widgets, choose descriptive names like ScoreText or IconImage so you can reference them easily in the graph. This separation — design in Designer and behavior in Graph — keeps UI development modular and maintainable.

keyIdea.title: Widget Blueprint
keyIdea.text: A UserWidget asset that packages visual widgets and Blueprint logic into one reusable UI component.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Widget Blueprint explained
Definition

Widget Blueprint

A reusable UserWidget asset that contains both visual widgets and a Blueprint graph for behavior.

Designer vs Graph
Designer: place and configure widgets. Graph: add events, bindings, and functions that change the UI at runtime.
Naming convention
Use descriptive names like ScoreText, IconImage so graph references are clear and maintainable.
Concrete scenario
WBP_PlayerHUD exposes UpdateHealth(int NewHP) in its Graph. When the player takes damage, the Character calls that function and the widget updates HealthText to reflect the new value.
Key Takeaway

Widget Blueprints bundle UI visuals and behavior in one asset, making interfaces modular and easy to reuse.

screens.title: Common widgets and panels
screens.narratorSegment: UMG provides many widget types, but a few are used frequently for HUDs. Text Block displays static or dynamic text and is lightweight for labels like "Health: 100". Image shows textures or materials and is commonly used for icons. For layout, panels organize children: Canvas Panel offers absolute positioning and anchors, making it ideal for HUDs that require precise placement relative to screen edges. Vertical Box and Horizontal Box stack children in columns or rows and are great for menus and lists where relative layout is preferred. When should you pick one over another? Use Canvas Panel when you need exact control and anchoring to corners or edges. Use Vertical or Horizontal Box when you want items to flow naturally and resize together. A misconception is to overuse Canvas for everything; for menus where elements should adapt to content size, boxes are simpler and more responsive. A practical example: create a Canvas Panel as the root for a HUD, add a Text Block named ScoreText and an Image for a coin. For a settings menu, prefer Vertical Box so buttons stack and spacing remains consistent when translated or resized. Which layout will keep your UI robust as you add more items?

keyIdea.title: Widget vs Panel
keyIdea.text: Choose widgets for content and panels for layout: Canvas for precise HUDs, Box widgets for flexible stacked layouts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Common widgets & panels
Comparison

Widgets and Panels

Text Block
Lightweight label for static or dynamic text like "Score: 0".
Image
Displays textures for icons and backgrounds; set SizeX/SizeY to control pixel dimensions.
Canvas Panel
Absolute positioning and anchors; best for HUD elements that attach to screen edges.
Vertical/Horizontal Box
Flow-based layout; items stack and resize together — ideal for menus and lists.
Concrete example
HUD: Canvas root → ScoreText (Text Block) anchored top-right → CoinImage (Image) anchored top-right with offsets. Menu: Vertical Box with buttons so adding new menu items keeps layout consistent.
Common mistake

Overusing Canvas leads to brittle menus. Prefer Box panels for lists and content-driven layouts.

screens.title: Canvas Panel and Anchors
screens.narratorSegment: Anchors in UMG define the point on a parent widget that a child will stick to, which is essential for responsive UI. The Canvas Panel supports anchors with presets like top-left, top-right, bottom-center, and custom rectangular anchors. When you anchor an element to a corner, its Position X and Position Y offsets determine the distance from that anchor. For instance, anchoring ScoreText to top-right and using Position X: -150 and Position Y: 20 keeps it near the corner regardless of resolution. Anchors influence how widgets scale and reposition during resolution changes; they do not automatically resize content unless you use relative anchors that stretch. A frequent beginner error is to set anchors but still rely on absolute pixel coordinates that break on different aspect ratios. Another pitfall is anchoring both the Image and Text incorrectly so they separate at runtime; ensure both share compatible anchors if they should stay together. Practice: set the coin Image and ScoreText to the top-right anchor, then adjust offsets to align them visually. Ask yourself: what happens if you anchor to center instead of top-right — how will offset signs change?

keyIdea.text: Anchors bind a widget's position to a screen edge or area; offsets then fine-tune the placement so elements remain consistent across resolutions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Canvas Panel & Anchors
Process Flow

Anchor, Offset, Test

Step 1 — Anchor
Select your widget and pick an anchor preset (top-right for a score HUD).
Step 2 — Offset
Adjust Position X/Y to fine-tune distance from the anchor point; negative X values often nudge left from the right anchor.
Step 3 — Test
Preview the widget at multiple aspect ratios in Designer or PIE to confirm consistency.
Visual example
Canvas Panel
Anchor: Top-Right
Position X: -150 · Position Y: 20
Common mistake

Using absolute pixel coordinates without anchors causes misalignment across resolutions; anchors plus offsets is the correct pattern.

screens.title: ZOrder and visual stacking
screens.narratorSegment: ZOrder controls the drawing order of widgets: widgets with higher ZOrder values are drawn later and therefore appear on top of widgets with lower values. This is especially important when UI elements overlap, like an icon partially covering a background panel or a temporary notification that should sit above the HUD. In the Details panel, each widget can receive a ZOrder integer. When two children share the same parent, compare their ZOrder to predict which will be visible above the other. A common confusion is assuming the visual tree order equals drawing order — child order and ZOrder interact, but explicit ZOrder makes intent clear. For example, place a translucent background rectangle at ZOrder 0 and assign the score label and coin icon ZOrder 1 so they remain visible. If a widget unexpectedly disappears behind another, check ZOrder first. Remember also that ZOrder is local to the parent panel; moving a widget to a different panel may change relative stacking. Practice setting ZOrder when designing overlapping elements so you can control visibility and avoid accidental occlusion at runtime. ZOrder and visual stacking means higher zorder values draw on top; use them intentionally to prevent accidental overlap and to guarantee visibility of important ui elements.. In practical terms, how drawing order controls which widget appears on top. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › ZOrder & stacking
Definition

ZOrder: control drawing order

Assign integer ZOrder values to children so higher numbers appear above lower ones when overlapping occurs.

Example
Background panel ZOrder 0 · ScoreText ZOrder 1 · CoinImage ZOrder 2 ensures icon sits above text and background.
Pitfall
Moving widgets between panels changes the stacking context; ZOrder is relative to the parent panel.
Quick check
If a widget is hidden behind another, increase its ZOrder or check parent hierarchy. Use ZOrder intentionally for popups, tooltips, and HUD icons.
Key Takeaway

ZOrder decides draw order; higher values render last and appear on top of lower ones.

screens.title: Create Widget and Add to Viewport
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a Widget Blueprint is only half the job — you must create an instance and add it to the viewport so it becomes visible. The typical place to do this is in your Player Controller or Player Character Blueprint on the Event BeginPlay node. The sequence is straightforward: from Event BeginPlay call Create Widget, choose your Widget Blueprint class (for example WBP_PlayerHUD), and set Owning Player to Get Player Controller. The Create Widget node returns a widget reference. From that return value call Add to Viewport; this attaches the widget to the screen's UI rendering so the player sees it. A persistent mistake is placing Create Widget without calling Add to Viewport, which leaves the widget in memory but not rendered. Another consideration is ownership: setting the Owning Player correctly ensures input and focus behave as expected in multiplayer or split-screen contexts. For testing, add a small debug print after Add to Viewport so you know the flow ran. Finally, remember to remove widgets or hide them when no longer needed to avoid clutter or performance costs. Create Widget and Add to Viewport means event beginplay → create widget (wbp) → add to viewport. without add to viewport the widget will not appear.. In practical terms, blueprint steps to display your widget blueprint at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Create Widget & Add to Viewport
Process Flow

Event BeginPlay → Create Widget → Add to Viewport

// Blueprint flow (visual nodes represented as pseudocode)
Event BeginPlay
  → Create Widget (Class: WBP_PlayerHUD, Owning Player: Get Player Controller)
      (Return Value: WBP_PlayerHUD Reference)
  → Add to Viewport (Target: WBP_PlayerHUD Reference)
Ownership
Set Owning Player to Get Player Controller so input focus and multiplayer behavior are correct.
Debug tip
Print a message after Add to Viewport to confirm the flow executed in PIE.
Common mistake
Forgetting Add to Viewport is the most common reason a created widget is invisible. Check the Create→Add chain first when a UI doesn't appear.
Key Takeaway

Create Widget returns an instance; Add to Viewport is required to render that instance on the player's screen.

screens.title: Blueprint pseudocode: showing a HUD
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact pseudocode representation of the Blueprint nodes you will use to show a HUD. Begin with Event BeginPlay in your Player Character or Player Controller. From there create a widget by selecting Create Widget and choosing WBP_GameHUD as the class. Set the Owning Player input to Get Player Controller. The Create Widget node returns a reference to the newly created widget instance. Immediately call Add to Viewport on that return value; Add to Viewport makes the widget visible. If you need to store the reference for later updates, save it in a variable on the Blueprint. For example you may store it as HUDWidget and later call HUDWidget→SetScore or HUDWidget→UpdateHealth. A common misconception is that Create Widget automatically attaches the widget. It does not. Also ensure the Blueprint containing this flow is actually active for the player; Event BeginPlay in a non-possessed actor will not run for the player. This walkthrough gives you a clear mental mapping from visual nodes to runtime behavior so you can implement it reliably in the editor. Blueprint pseudocode: showing a HUD means event beginplay triggers create widget; save its return value if you need to update the ui later, then call add to viewport to show it.. In practical terms, a readable code-style view of the create widget → add to viewport flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Performance & common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: UMG is flexible, but to keep performance healthy you should avoid creating many complex widgets every frame. Common beginner mistakes include creating duplicates of the same widget, forgetting to remove or hide widgets when no longer needed, and using deeply nested widgets when a simpler layout would suffice. If you have a heavy visual element that rarely changes, consider using a Retainer Box to cache its rendered output. For controlling size consistently, use a Size Box to limit a child widget’s dimensions. Also, test on lower-end hardware if your game targets it; high widget counts and expensive material effects can reduce frame rate. Another mistake is not setting Owning Player correctly, which can lead to focus or input issues in multiplayer or split-screen. Lastly, always test anchors across multiple aspect ratios before finalizing placement. For optimization, create widgets only when needed and destroy or remove them when they are not visible. These practices keep your UI responsive and avoid common runtime surprises. Keep UMG efficient and reliable

Avoid frequent creation
Don’t spawn many complex widgets every frame; create when needed and reuse or cache.

screens.title: Troubleshooting & assessment
screens.narratorSegment: When a Widget Blueprint doesn't appear at runtime, follow a short diagnostic checklist. First, confirm the Create Widget node runs by adding a debug print or breakpoint on Event BeginPlay. If Create Widget runs, ensure Add to Viewport is called on the returned reference — without it the widget will not render. Next, verify the correct Widget Class is selected in Create Widget. If anchors were used incorrectly, the widget might be off-screen; check anchor presets and offsets in the Designer. Also examine ZOrder — a lower ZOrder may be hidden behind other UI elements. If input or focus seems wrong, check Owning Player is set to Get Player Controller for the intended player. For performance issues where UI appears but lags, inspect whether many widgets are being updated every frame; consider Retainer Box and Size Box for optimization. An assessment question you can use: “You created WBP_MainMenu but it does not show — which node did you likely forget?” The expected answer is Add to Viewport after Create Widget. Use this checklist to systematically isolate and fix UI visibility problems.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn what Unreal Motion Graphics, or UMG, does and how to use a Widget Blueprint to create a simple HUD that appears during gameplay. UMG is the visual editor inside Unreal Engine for building menus, inventory screens, and heads-up displays without writing C++ code. You'll see how a Widget Blueprint holds UI widgets, how panel widgets like the Canvas Panel control layout, and why anchoring is crucial for responsive positioning across screen sizes. We'll also cover the runtime steps: creating the widget in Blueprint, then adding it to the viewport so the player can see it. A short example you will implement shows a score label and a coin icon anchored to the top-right of the screen. Understanding this flow — design, anchor, create, and add — ensures the UI looks consistent in editor and at runtime. By the end you will be able to make a basic HUD, test it in Play In Editor, and avoid common mistakes such as forgetting to add the widget to the viewport or misusing anchors. Think about one UI you need in your game and how anchoring would keep it stable across window sizes.

By the end of this chapter you will understand UMG's role and be able to create and display a Widget Blueprint. First, you'll know what UMG is and why it is used to build HUDs, menus, and interactive screens without C++ code. Second, you'll create and configure a Widget Blueprint, place common widgets such as Text Block and Image, and arrange them inside panels like the Canvas Panel. Third, you'll apply anchoring and layout principles so your UI remains responsive across resolutions. Finally, you'll connect your UI to gameplay by creating the widget in Blueprint and using Add to Viewport so it renders during play. Each objective maps to a hands-on practice: design a simple HUD, set anchors, and add the widget at Event BeginPlay. These skills matter because players on different devices must see consistent UI, and Blueprints let you iterate quickly. A quick misconception to avoid: creating a widget asset is not enough — you must also add it to the viewport. Keep that in mind as your verification milestone.

These objectives map directly to tasks you will do during the hands-on activity. You will create a Widget Blueprint asset and add Text and Image widgets to a Canvas Panel. You will practice setting anchors so a 'Score: 0' label and a coin image remain pinned to the top-right corner on varied screen sizes. You will then open your Player Character or Player Controller Blueprint, hook Event BeginPlay to Create Widget with your new Blueprint class, and call Add to Viewport on the returned reference. The why: players experience inconsistent HUDs when anchors are ignored, and widgets that are created but not added remain invisible. A typical beginner mistake is skipping Add to Viewport; another is anchoring the element to the wrong corner so it drifts off-screen on other aspect ratios. Your verified milestone is simple: run Play In Editor and confirm the HUD appears in the expected position on at least two different aspect ratios. If it does, you have successfully completed the core workflow and can iterate further by adding dynamic text updates and icons.

UMG stands for Unreal Motion Graphics. It is the built-in visual UI system inside Unreal Engine that lets you create menus, HUDs, and interactive screens using Widget Blueprints. Widget Blueprints are assets that contain widgets — the building blocks like text blocks, images, buttons, and progress bars — arranged in panel widgets that control layout. The major practical advantage is iteration speed: designers and scripters can place widgets visually and hook up behavior in Blueprint graphs without compiling engine code. For example, if you need a pause menu or a health display, you can drag a Text Block and an Image into a Widget Blueprint and then update the text from game logic. A common misconception is thinking UMG is only for simple overlays; in fact it supports complex, data-driven UIs, animations, and binding to game variables. However, it’s also important to be mindful of performance: many complex widgets rendered every frame can affect framerate, so use caching or Retainer Boxes when needed. To practice, create a new UserWidget and add a Text Block named HealthText, set default text, and preview in the Designer tab. How would you use UMG to make your game's main menu responsive and extendable?

A Widget Blueprint is a special Blueprint asset whose root is typically a panel widget and whose children are UMG widgets such as Text Block, Image, Button, Progress Bar, and more. Think of it as a container that both defines the visual arrangement and exposes a graph where you add logic to react to input or update text and images. In the Designer tab you drag widgets into panels and set properties like name, text, brush textures, size, anchors, and ZOrder. In the Graph tab you can create bindings, events, and functions that change widget properties at runtime. For example, a WBP_PlayerHUD could expose an UpdateHealth function that accepts an integer and sets the HealthText to "Health: " plus that value. A common misconception is that widgets created in the Content Browser automatically appear; they do not. You must create an instance at runtime and call Add to Viewport. When naming widgets, choose descriptive names like ScoreText or IconImage so you can reference them easily in the graph. This separation — design in Designer and behavior in Graph — keeps UI development modular and maintainable.

UMG provides many widget types, but a few are used frequently for HUDs. Text Block displays static or dynamic text and is lightweight for labels like "Health: 100". Image shows textures or materials and is commonly used for icons. For layout, panels organize children: Canvas Panel offers absolute positioning and anchors, making it ideal for HUDs that require precise placement relative to screen edges. Vertical Box and Horizontal Box stack children in columns or rows and are great for menus and lists where relative layout is preferred. When should you pick one over another? Use Canvas Panel when you need exact control and anchoring to corners or edges. Use Vertical or Horizontal Box when you want items to flow naturally and resize together. A misconception is to overuse Canvas for everything; for menus where elements should adapt to content size, boxes are simpler and more responsive. A practical example: create a Canvas Panel as the root for a HUD, add a Text Block named ScoreText and an Image for a coin. For a settings menu, prefer Vertical Box so buttons stack and spacing remains consistent when translated or resized. Which layout will keep your UI robust as you add more items?

Anchors in UMG define the point on a parent widget that a child will stick to, which is essential for responsive UI. The Canvas Panel supports anchors with presets like top-left, top-right, bottom-center, and custom rectangular anchors. When you anchor an element to a corner, its Position X and Position Y offsets determine the distance from that anchor. For instance, anchoring ScoreText to top-right and using Position X: -150 and Position Y: 20 keeps it near the corner regardless of resolution. Anchors influence how widgets scale and reposition during resolution changes; they do not automatically resize content unless you use relative anchors that stretch. A frequent beginner error is to set anchors but still rely on absolute pixel coordinates that break on different aspect ratios. Another pitfall is anchoring both the Image and Text incorrectly so they separate at runtime; ensure both share compatible anchors if they should stay together. Practice: set the coin Image and ScoreText to the top-right anchor, then adjust offsets to align them visually. Ask yourself: what happens if you anchor to center instead of top-right — how will offset signs change?

ZOrder controls the drawing order of widgets: widgets with higher ZOrder values are drawn later and therefore appear on top of widgets with lower values. This is especially important when UI elements overlap, like an icon partially covering a background panel or a temporary notification that should sit above the HUD. In the Details panel, each widget can receive a ZOrder integer. When two children share the same parent, compare their ZOrder to predict which will be visible above the other. A common confusion is assuming the visual tree order equals drawing order — child order and ZOrder interact, but explicit ZOrder makes intent clear. For example, place a translucent background rectangle at ZOrder 0 and assign the score label and coin icon ZOrder 1 so they remain visible. If a widget unexpectedly disappears behind another, check ZOrder first. Remember also that ZOrder is local to the parent panel; moving a widget to a different panel may change relative stacking. Practice setting ZOrder when designing overlapping elements so you can control visibility and avoid accidental occlusion at runtime. ZOrder and visual stacking means higher zorder values draw on top; use them intentionally to prevent accidental overlap and to guarantee visibility of important ui elements.. In practical terms, how drawing order controls which widget appears on top. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing a Widget Blueprint is only half the job — you must create an instance and add it to the viewport so it becomes visible. The typical place to do this is in your Player Controller or Player Character Blueprint on the Event BeginPlay node. The sequence is straightforward: from Event BeginPlay call Create Widget, choose your Widget Blueprint class (for example WBP_PlayerHUD), and set Owning Player to Get Player Controller. The Create Widget node returns a widget reference. From that return value call Add to Viewport; this attaches the widget to the screen's UI rendering so the player sees it. For testing, add a small debug print after Add to Viewport so you know the flow ran. Finally, remember to remove widgets or hide them when no longer needed to avoid clutter or performance costs.
